title: Equations and inequalities: meaning and solution sets
summary: Distinguish equations from inequalities, test candidate values and reason about equivalent statements.
objectives: Classify algebraic statements as equations or inequalities and identify their solution sets.
Test whether a value satisfies a statement by substitution.
Create equivalent statements by preserving balance or order.

blocks.text: An equation states that two expressions are equal. It may be true for one value, several values, every allowed value or no value. An inequality compares expressions using <, >, ≤ or ≥, so its solution is often a range rather than a single number. The solution set contains every value that makes the original statement true.

Substitution is the safest way to test a proposed solution. Replace every occurrence of the variable, evaluate both sides independently and then compare them. For an equation the values must be equal; for an inequality the stated order must hold. A failed test proves the candidate is not in the solution set.

Adding or subtracting the same expression on both sides preserves an equation and an inequality. Multiplying or dividing an equation by a non-zero number preserves equality. For inequalities, multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the comparison sign; this rule is explored fully in the next lesson.

Do not stop after testing one side: evaluate both sides and compare them. A boundary value satisfies ≤ or ≥ but not < or >. An equation such as 2x + 1 = 2x + 3 has no solution, while 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2 is true for every x; neither is a mistake.

sections.title: Worked example: check a candidate

content.text: Substitute x = 4 into the left side and evaluate it.
The left side equals the right side, 10, so x = 4 is a solution.

sections.verification_note: The original equation becomes 10 = 10, a true statement.

sections.title: Worked example: test values in an inequality

prompt.text: Which of x = 1, 2 and 3 are in the solution set of 2x + 3 < 9?

content.text: Substitute each value into the left side.
5 < 9 and 7 < 9 are true, but 9 < 9 is false, because 9 is equal to 9, not less than it.
So x = 1 and x = 2 are in the solution set, and x = 3 is not.

sections.verification_note: Solving gives 2x < 6, so x < 3, which agrees: 1 and 2 are less than 3, and 3 is not.

sections.title: Worked example: make an identity

prompt.text: Find k so that (2k + 1)x − 4 = 7x − 4 is true for every value of x.

content.text: An identity needs the same coefficient of x and the same constant on both sides. The constants are already −4 on both sides.

sections.verification_note: With k = 3, both sides are 7x − 4, so every value of x makes the statement true.

prompt.text: Which whole number x satisfies both 3x − 2 > 4 and x < 4?

feedback.text: 3x − 2 > 4 gives 3x > 6, so x > 2. The only whole number greater than 2 and less than 4 is 3.

blocks.text: An equation is true for particular values; an inequality is usually true for a range of values. The solution set is every value that makes the original statement true.

Test a value by substituting it into both sides and comparing. Keep a statement equivalent by doing the same to both sides, and reverse an inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
